Strongest lightweight match: [Revisiting Graph Projections (2025)](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.09209v1) combines normalized user–item graph projection with directed, inverse-distance-weighted purchase transitions; recommendations come from weighted graph neighbors, without pretrained weights. Important limitation: its sparsity regularizer uses product-category transitions, unavailable here. A training-only item-transition variant is feasible; replacing category smoothing with title/description clusters would be an experimental adaptation. The paper explicitly treats temporal relationships as a proxy for complementarity, not verified relationship labels.

Two relevant architectural ideas: [SComGNN (AAAI 2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28734) combines low-pass and mid-pass graph filters to capture both relevance and dissimilarity, suggesting that ordinary similarity smoothing can miss complementary relationships. [TransGAT (ICDM 2024)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10884336/) encodes behavioral direction and jointly learns complementary/substitute graphs. Its reliance on relation graphs limits direct transfer when only chronological histories and text are available.

Suggested hypothesis to validate: retain SASRec personalization and add a gated directed-transition score, using separate source/target item embeddings trained from scratch. Compare immediate versus short-window transitions, symmetric versus asymmetric scoring, and optional TF–IDF or learned bag-of-words title/description features for sparse items. These are proposed adaptations, not established findings from the cited papers. Text similarity should provide auxiliary evidence rather than automatically identify substitutes; purchase order likewise cannot establish compatibility or complementarity. Select changes using the pinned four-category macro validation HR@10, without claiming improvements before measurement.
